Should You Use the Builder's Preferred Lender? New Construction on the Grand Strand

Buying a new home in Myrtle Beach? The builder's incentive is only half the story. Here's how to compare the whole loan.

Paul Hankins
Founder & Broker · NMLS #281393

You don't have to use the builder's preferred lender. Builders on the Grand Strand often offer an incentive, like money toward closing costs, if you finance with their lender. Sometimes that's a good deal. Often the incentive looks bigger than it is once you see the whole loan. The only way to know is to compare full Loan Estimates side by side, and that's what a broker does.

Do you have to use the builder's lender?

No. Federal law doesn't let a builder require you to use a lender it's affiliated with. A builder can offer you a discount for using its lender, but the offer has to be optional. Under the same federal rules, a discount like that has to be a true discount, not made up through higher costs somewhere else in the deal. And if the builder has an ownership stake in the lender, it has to tell you.

The incentive is there to steer you to the builder's lender. Turning it down is always your choice.

How builder incentives work

The offer usually looks like one of these:

  • a credit toward your closing costs;
  • money to lower your interest rate for a while, called a buydown;
  • upgrades in the house, like flooring or appliances.

Fannie Mae and other loan programs cap how much a builder can put toward your costs. The cap depends on the loan and your down payment, so a very large incentive may not all be usable.

The catch: compare the whole loan, not the incentive

An incentive is one number. Your loan has several:

CompareWhy it matters
Interest rateA small difference in rate can cost more over a few years than a one-time credit saves.
Lender fees (origination charges)A credit at closing doesn't help much if the lender's fees are higher to start with.
Cash to closeThe bottom line you bring to the table, after every credit.
Loan type and termsThe best program for you may not be one the builder's lender offers.

Every lender has to give you a Loan Estimate within three business days of your application. It's a standard three-page form, so two lenders' offers line up line by line. Ask for one from the builder's lender and one from us, and lay them side by side.

An example. A builder in Carolina Forest offers a $10,000 closing cost credit if the buyers use its lender. The buyers ask BrickWood for a Loan Estimate too. Line by line, they see the rate, the fees and the cash to close on both. Sometimes the builder's deal wins. Sometimes a lower rate somewhere else is worth more than the credit over the years they plan to own the home. Either way, they choose with the numbers in front of them, not the sales pitch.

Why a broker, not one lender

The builder's preferred lender is one lender, and it works with that builder on sale after sale. BrickWood is a mortgage broker. We take your loan to several lenders and show you what each one offers, so you see the market instead of one quote.

That matters most when your situation isn't simple: you're self-employed, you're buying a second home, you're selling another house, or you're close to a loan limit. The builder's lender has one set of programs. We have access to many.

Read the financing section of the builder's contract

New construction contracts are written by the builder. Before you sign, look for:

  • The incentive terms. What exactly you get, and what happens to it if you use another lender.
  • Financing deadlines. How long you have to get approved. Get pre-qualified before you sign, so the clock isn't a surprise.
  • The deposit. When your earnest money becomes non-refundable.

Your real estate agent or attorney can walk you through the contract. We can tell you whether the financing timeline works for your loan.

When the builder's lender might be the right call

Sometimes it is. If the incentive is large, your situation is simple, and the full Loan Estimate holds up next to ours, take the deal. The point isn't to never use the builder's lender. It's to never use it without comparing.

Builder lender questions

Can a builder make you use their lender?

No. Under federal law, a builder can't require you to use a lender it's affiliated with. It can offer an optional incentive for using that lender, and it must disclose an ownership stake in the lender.

Is the builder's preferred lender cheaper?

Sometimes, but an incentive is only one number. Compare the interest rate, the lender fees and the cash to close on full Loan Estimates from the builder's lender and at least one other lender.

Can I keep the builder incentive if I use my own lender?

It depends on the builder. Many tie the incentive to their lender. Read the incentive terms in the contract, then compare what you'd save with each lender.

How do I compare two mortgage offers?

Ask each lender for a Loan Estimate. Lenders must give you one within three business days of your application, and the standard form lets you compare the rate, fees and cash to close line by line.
